Text: How to Train for Skiing and Ski Mountaineering (Stomp It Pod, w/ Uphill Athlete)
Layer muscular endurance (loaded uphill work) on top of your aerobic base — not instead of your easy volume
Track weekly vertical gain/loss and compare it against the event's per-mile elevation demands
Build a general strength foundation before progressing into heavier loaded/uphill-specific work
Push your longest efforts toward race-like time-on-feet and terrain over the coming weeks
Address any nagging injury or fatigue signal now, while there's still time to adjust the plan
Reduce volume while keeping some intensity/frequency — a taper isn't just stopping
Skip any new 'confidence-boosting' hard efforts or big vert days this close to the event
Give any lingering injury real attention now, not during the event
Redirect the extra time and energy toward sleep, gear prep, and mental rehearsal instead of more training stress
Bank at least a year of consistent, patiently-built training before treating an ultra as the goal, not the stretch
Know your target distance's minimum weekly hours during peak training — 6 hrs/week for a 50K or 50-miler, 9 hrs/week for a 100K or 100-miler — and build your schedule to actually hit it
Increase weekly volume gradually and don't skip cutback weeks — big, fast jumps in mileage are the most common way new ultrarunners get hurt
Map out realistically where the training time will come from before you commit — work, family, and sleep don't pause for a training block
Build your support system before race day — a training partner, family who understands the time commitment, or a coach
Practice a run/walk strategy in training now — walking hills isn't failure, it's how almost every ultrarunner actually finishes
Pick one specific race you're genuinely excited about and commit to it, rather than staying vague about "doing an ultra someday"
Build up gradually — day hikes, then overnights, then multi-day trips — rather than jumping straight to your goal hike
Train with your pack loaded to actual trip weight, not empty or lightly loaded — this is what most first-timers get wrong
Do at least one back-to-back multi-day trip before your goal hike, so you know what day 2 and 3 actually feel like
Pick a well-established, appropriately-scoped route for a first attempt — save the remote, technical routes for once you have miles under you
Build a real budget — resupply, lodging/permits, gear, and an emergency buffer — running out of money ends more thru-hikes than injuries do
Line up your support system now — someone to manage resupply boxes and check in on your progress
Commit to one specific trail you're genuinely excited about, rather than staying vague about "doing a long hike someday"
Set aside real weekly time for route, gear, and resupply research — treat planning as part of the training, not an afterthought
Build your aerobic base first — roughly 85% of training volume should stay below your aerobic threshold, with intensity added only once that base is built
Progress gradually and continuously — big jumps in volume or intensity are the fastest route to injury or overtraining, not to fitness
Train muscular endurance specific to carrying a loaded pack for hours, not just raw gym strength — that's what actually gets taxed on the mountain
Take a mountaineering course or hire a guide to learn ice axe, crampon, and rope skills before going unguided — these aren't skills to learn for the first time on your objective
Pick a non-technical objective well within your current skill level for a first attempt — save harder routes for once you've built real mountain experience
Get avalanche safety training (AIARE Level 1) and practice with your beacon, shovel, and probe until it's second nature, if your route crosses avalanche terrain
Line up a partner with matching skills for roped sections — technical terrain is a team sport, and a mismatched partner is its own risk factor
Decide your turnaround criteria before you leave, not on the mountain — the turnaround call is consistently cited as the hardest and most important decision in mountaineering
Get wilderness first aid training, or make sure someone on your team has it — you may be hours or days from professional help
Learn to read mountain weather — cloud buildup, wind shifts, pressure changes — so you can make a real go/no-go call instead of just hoping the forecast holds
Build your aerobic base first, the same principle behind all Uphill Athlete training — race-pace intensity only pays off once that foundation is there
Structured skimo plans generally run 6–10 hours/week at peak — make sure your schedule can actually support that before race day, not just in theory
Get comfortable on ungroomed, off-piste, and expert terrain before race day — many courses intentionally leave the groomed runs
Train on your actual race gear beforehand — race skis and boots behave very differently from touring setups, and race day is the wrong time to find that out
Practice transitions — skins off, boots to ski mode — until they're automatic; fumbled transitions cost more time than most people expect
Plan your recovery as deliberately as your training, especially around back-to-back race weekends — fatigue management is part of the program, not an afterthought
Practice with your beacon, shovel, and probe until you're genuinely competent, not just equipped — many races require this gear for a reason
Read up on the actual race format beforehand — transition zones, mandatory gear checks, how the course is marked — so none of it is a surprise on race morning

Text: Gradually increasing the altitude you sleep at is the best way to prevent altitude illness. For a low-risk ascent, take at least two days to reach a sleeping altitude of 8,200-9,800 ft, then climb no more than 1,600 ft per night and add a rest day for every 3,300 ft of sleeping-altitude gain. Relevance: Supports allowing time to acclimatize when the event's elevation is well above where you live and train.
Source: Luks AM, et al. Wilderness Medical Society clinical practice guidelines for the prevention and treatment of acute altitude illness: 2019 update. Wilderness Environ Med. 2019;30(4S):S3-S18.

Text: Heat acclimatization through repeated exercise-heat exposures over one to two weeks is described as the most effective intervention against heat's impairment of endurance exercise; the statement also recommends hydration and cooling strategies. Text: Athletes who are unacclimatized, dehydrated, recently ill, or taking certain medications face higher risk of exertional heat illness. Text: Blisters come from friction on the skin. Source: Knapik JJ, et al. Friction blisters: pathophysiology, prevention and treatment. Sports Med. 1995.

Text: Survey of 500 entrants in two 161-km (100-mile) trail ultramarathons: the main performance-limiting problems were nausea/vomiting, blisters and muscle pain, and nausea/vomiting was the most common reason given for not finishing (23% of non-finishers). Source: Hoffman MD, Fogard K. Factors related to successful completion of a 161-km ultramarathon. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2011;6(1):25-37.

Text: Study of 1,247 avalanche burials in Canada and Switzerland (1980-2005): about 46% of buried people survived, survival depended heavily on how long they stayed buried, and the authors emphasize extrication ideally within 10 minutes. Source: Haegeli P, Falk M, Brugger H, Etter HJ, Boyd J. Comparison of avalanche survival patterns in Canada and Switzerland. CMAJ. 2011.

Early recognition and rapid cooling reduce illness severity and death, and the early signs can be subtle and easy to miss. Relevance: Covers exertional heat illness, including heat stroke, among the serious conditions listed.
Source: Armstrong LE, Casa DJ, Millard-Stafford M, Moran DS, Pyne SW, Roberts WO. American College of Sports Medicine position stand: exertional heat illness during training and competition. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2007;39(3):556-572.

Text: Consensus statement from 17 international experts on exercise-associated hyponatremia (low blood sodium): it covers how common it is, its causes, diagnosis, treatment and prevention, and describes it as a preventable and treatable fluid imbalance. Relevance: Covers exercise-associated hyponatremia among the serious conditions listed.
Source: Hew-Butler T, Rosner MH, Fowkes-Godek S, et al. Statement of the Third International Exercise-Associated Hyponatremia Consensus Development Conference, Carlsbad, California, 2015. Clin J Sport Med. 2015;25(4):303-320.

Text: Review of how athletes distribute effort during races: even pacing helps in events longer than about two minutes. For events over four hours the review found limited evidence on the best strategy, with well-trained athletes typically slowing progressively. Relevance: Supports having a pacing plan; note the review found limited evidence on the best pacing strategy for events over four hours.
Source: Abbiss CR, Laursen PB. Describing and understanding pacing strategies during athletic competition. Sports Med. 2008;38(3):239-252.

Text: Meta-analysis of 99 studies: massage was the most effective recovery technique for soreness and perceived fatigue, and active recovery, compression garments, water immersion and cold therapy also reduced soreness. Relevance: Not ultramarathon-specific, and it evaluates recovery techniques rather than sleep or nutrition.
Source: Dupuy O, Douzi W, Theurot D, et al. An evidence-based approach for choosing post-exercise recovery techniques to reduce markers of muscle damage, soreness, fatigue, and inflammation: a systematic review with meta-analysis. Front Physiol. 2018;9:403.

Text: In a 2024 cross-sectional field survey of 586 day hikers and 68 trail runners in Rocky Mountain National Park, only a minority met the authors' definition of 'wilderness prepared' (at least 1 liter of water, 7 of 13 of the Ten Essentials, a map or equivalent, and either two rescue devices or 8 of 15 first-aid items). Press coverage of the published version reports about 15.7% of day hikers and 25% of trail runners met it. Roughly a quarter did not tell anyone their plans, and more wilderness days per year and prior wilderness injury were associated with higher preparedness. Relevance: Shows that carrying backup items such as navigation, extra layers and emergency equipment is uncommon even among experienced recreationists, which supports asking about it directly. It was a survey of what people carried, not a study of whether carrying more gear prevents incidents.
Source: Lambert JT, Hamer DH, Weckstein TN, Wellenius GA. Know before you go! A field survey of the preparedness of wilderness day hikers and trail runners in Rocky Mountain National Park. medRxiv preprint 2025 (doi 10.1101/2025.09.23.25336486); published in Wilderness & Environmental Medicine, 2026 (we read the preprint and press coverage, not the published article, so check figures against the published version).
Evidence Type: Cross-sectional survey (654 participants; preprint plus 2026 publication)

Text: In a five-year prospective surveillance study of National Outdoor Leadership School students and instructors, injuries occurred at 2.3 per 1,000 person-days and illnesses at 1.5 per 1,000 person-days. Sprains, strains and soft-tissue injuries made up 80% of injuries, and 39% of injuries and illnesses required evacuation. The authors concluded that wilderness medical efforts should concentrate on hygiene and on musculoskeletal and soft-tissue injuries, and that wilderness activities can be conducted relatively safely. Relevance: Supports planning for self-care and evacuation, since a large share of backcountry problems are minor injuries and illnesses that still end trips. The population was guided course participants, not ultrarunners or climbers on their own.
Source: Gentile DA, et al. Wilderness injuries and illnesses. Ann Emerg Med. 1992 Jul. (Volume and pages not verified.)

Text: Accidents in North American Climbing is published annually by the American Alpine Club (since 1948) and compiles first-person and rescuer reports of the year's most significant and teachable climbing accidents, with analysis of what went wrong. Its archive holds more than 5,000 reports. Relevance: A source of case-based lessons for mountaineering and skimo contingency planning. These are curated incident reports, not a systematic or complete count, so we cite no statistic from it and it cannot show how common any cause is.
Source: American Alpine Club. Accidents in North American Climbing (annual publication since 1948). About page.
Evidence Type: Incident reports (curated case reports, not a study)

Text: McCammon analyzed 715 recreational avalanche accidents in the United States (1972-2003) and described six behavioral 'heuristic traps' (familiarity, acceptance, consistency, expert halo, tracks/scarcity, social facilitation). In 73% of accidents three or more obvious danger indicators were present, almost half of the parties included formally trained people, and the link between trap cues and exposure grew with training level. The author states the results show correlations only, cannot establish causation, and should be viewed as preliminary. Relevance: Supports deciding turnaround or stopping criteria in advance, since the 'consistency' trap describes people holding to an earlier decision despite new warning signs. Avalanche accidents are not ultrarunning, so this supports the premise only.
Source: McCammon I. Heuristic traps in recreational avalanche accidents: evidence and implications. Avalanche News. 2004;68 (Spring).
Evidence Type: Retrospective accident analysis (715 US avalanche accidents; avalanche-specific)

Text: In an online survey of 693 people in Norway, 427 reported having been temporarily disoriented outdoors, most for a few minutes (42%) or 30-60 minutes (46%). Among the 283 who described how they recovered, the most common approaches were using maps, tools or technology (48.4%; digital maps 22.6%, paper maps 14.8%) and reading the surroundings (44.9%), followed by movement strategies such as trail-following or backtracking (40.6%). The authors note the data are self-reported, skew toward ages 20-39 and a Norwegian, well-educated sample, and the coding was not tested for inter-rater reliability. Relevance: Shows that getting disoriented outdoors is common and that people most often recover using a map or device, which supports asking whether you have a backup navigation plan. This study describes how people recover, not how often a faulty mental map causes getting lost.
Source: Wattne OE, Volden F. Waylosing and wayfinding in the outdoors: a typology of wayfinding approaches to problem-solving when temporarily lost. The Journal of Navigation. 2024;76(6):603-626.
Evidence Type: Cross-sectional online survey (693 respondents, Norway; self-reported)

Text: In a representative telephone survey of 783 German-speaking adults, people described how they find their way using the Wayfinding Strategy Scale, a self-report measure of route-based strategies (following remembered landmarks and turns) and orientation strategies (a map-like sense of direction and layout). Most people used both strategies or neither rather than preferring one. Over a third of the population, mostly under age 35, did not successfully use either strategy, and the authors suggest this may reflect reliance on navigation aids. Higher education, being male and lower urbanization were associated with higher orientation scores, and dizziness or vertigo lowered both. Relevance: Supports asking how well you know the route, because knowing a route (landmarks and layout) is the basis of both strategies the study describes. It did not test outdoor or ultra routes, or whether route familiarity reduces getting lost.
Source: Ulrich S, Grill E, Flanagin VL. Who gets lost and why: a representative cross-sectional survey on sociodemographic and vestibular determinants of wayfinding strategies. PLoS ONE. 2019;14(1):e0204781.
Evidence Type: Cross-sectional survey (783 adults, Germany; self-reported, everyday wayfinding)

Text: A retrospective review of 754 search-and-rescue (SAR) or medical-need incidents in Baxter State Park, Maine (1992-2014). Traumatic injuries started 51% of incidents and late or lost parties another 30%. Slips or falls while hiking caused 67% of injuries, and 84.4% of acute need (where applicable) occurred while descending rather than ascending. Fatigue was the most commonly reported medical emergency (66% of medical SAR events) and a contributor to other injuries. Relevance: Supports treating descending as a risk of its own, since most acute need in this park occurred on the way down. It was a single park, not ultra events, and did not measure elevation loss directly. Records describe who needed rescue, not everyone who got into trouble, and they do not isolate causes such as a faulty mental map.
Source: Welter CR, Sholl JM, Strout TD, Woodard B. Epidemiology of search and rescue in Baxter State Park: dangers of descent and fatigue. Wilderness Environ Med. 2015;26(4):549-554.
Evidence Type: Retrospective review of SAR reports (754 incidents; one US park; hikers)

Text: A retrospective review of 1,088 backcountry medical calls to Yosemite Search and Rescue (2000-2009), plus a survey of patients assisted in 2007-2009. Extremity pain was the chief complaint in 53% of cases and 46% of incidents occurred while hiking on a trail. In the patient survey, 54% described themselves as experts at the activity, 14.4% felt underprepared and 13% felt better gear would have prevented the incident. Appropriate footwear and sufficient water were the items patients most often said would have helped. The authors concluded many patients reported being experienced, well prepared and physically fit. Relevance: Patients most often named footwear and water as the items that would have helped, which supports checking footwear fit. The finding is self-reported after the fact, and extremity pain was the most common complaint. Records describe who needed rescue, not everyone who got into trouble, and they do not isolate causes such as a faulty mental map.
Source: Boore SM, Bock D. Ten years of search and rescue in Yosemite National Park: examining the past for future prevention. Wilderness Environ Med. 2013;24(1):2-7.
Evidence Type: Retrospective review plus patient survey (1,088 calls; one US park; self-reported)

Text: An analysis of National Park Service SAR data from 1992 to 2007: 65,439 incidents involving 78,488 people, with 2,659 fatalities and 24,288 ill or injured people. Hiking accounted for 48% of rescues and 22.8% of fatalities. Relevance: Hiking was the most common activity in national-park rescues, which supports knowing in advance how to reach help. These are US national park records, not ultra events. Records describe who needed rescue, not everyone who got into trouble, and they do not isolate causes such as a faulty mental map.
Source: Heggie TW, Amundson ME. Dead men walking: search and rescue in US National Parks. Wilderness Environ Med. 2009;20(3):244-249.
Evidence Type: Retrospective analysis of national SAR database (65,439 incidents; US national parks)
